bibliographic.title: Artificial Intelligence–Based Chatbots for Promoting Health Behavioral Changes: Systematic Review
bibliographic.authors: Abhishek Aggarwal; Cheuk Chi Tam; Dezhi Wu; Xiaoming Li; Shan Qiao
bibliographic.citation_apa: Aggarwal, A., Tam, C. C., Wu, D., Li, X., & Qiao, S. (2023). Artificial intelligence–based chatbots for promoting health behavioral changes: Systematic review. Journal of Medical Internet Research, 25, e40789. https://doi.org/10.2196/40789

methodology.study_design: systematic review with quality appraisal using CASP and CONSORT-AI checklists
methodology.sample_description: 15 empirical studies evaluating feasibility or efficacy of AI chatbots for health behavior change, published 1980–2022
methodology.technology_context: AI-driven conversational chatbots using ML, NLP, deep learning, and platforms such as IBM Watson Assistant; not LLM-specific

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article is a PRISMA systematic review of AI chatbots for health behavior change in a regulated healthcare domain and reports monitoring, deployment, and interaction data collection. However, the provided text does not center on conversational governance, accountability frameworks, guardrails, observability, audit, human oversight, or LLM-based systems; its primary objective is feasibility and efficacy of behavior-change interventions.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Python triage scored as central_candidate, but full-text evidence shows primary focus on health behavior change efficacy rather than conversational governance in LLM systems; manual adjudication needed on scope fit.

appraisal.notes: Clear PRISMA systematic review with multi-database search and structured quality appraisal (CASP, CONSORT-AI). Authors acknowledge moderate to high risk of internal validity, insufficient description of AI techniques, and generalizability limits. Ethics/reflexivity is not substantively addressed in the provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: Methodologically coherent systematic review with transparent limitations, but direct relevance to conversational governance in LLM systems in regulated environments is low because governance is not a primary analytic focus and LLMs are not specifically examined.

coding.theme: Efficacy and feasibility of AI chatbots for health behavior change
coding.subtheme: Intervention design, monitoring, and deployment in healthcare chatbots

synthesis.main_claim: AI chatbots show promising efficacy for health behavior change across diverse populations, but evidence on feasibility, acceptability, and usability is mixed and conclusions require caution due to validity and reporting limitations.
synthesis.contribution: Synthesizes 15 empirical studies on AI chatbot interventions for health behaviors using PRISMA, identifying common behavior-change strategies (goal setting, monitoring, feedback) and scalability via accessible platforms, while appraising study quality with CASP and CONSORT-AI.
synthesis.limitations: Moderate to high risk of internal validity, insufficient description of AI techniques, and limited generalizability; authors call for more robust randomized controlled trials.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as borderline or supporting contextual evidence on healthcare chatbot interventions, monitoring of interaction data, and deployment practices; not suitable as central evidence on conversational governance or LLM-specific governance mechanisms.

evidence.claim: Article is a systematic review of AI chatbots for health behavior change following PRISMA
evidence.excerpt: The aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the feasibility, efficacy, and intervention characteristics of AI chatbots for promoting health behavior change.
The screening, extraction, and analysis of the identified articles were performed by following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines.
Finally, 15 articles met the inclusion criteria and were selected for this review (Figure 1).

evidence.claim: Inclusion criteria require AI/ML/NLP-based chatbots, not LLM-specific
evidence.excerpt: chatbots developed upon existing AI platforms (eg, IBM Watson Assistant [IBM Corp]) or AI algorithms, such as ML, deep learning, natural language understanding, and NLP
Artificial intelligence (AI)–based chatbots can offer personalized, engaging, and on-demand health promotion interventions.
AI-driven chatbots (AI chatbots) are conversational agents that mimic human interaction through written, oral, and visual forms of communication with a user

evidence.claim: Interaction data collection and monitoring on chatbot platform
evidence.excerpt: Real-time user-chatbot interaction data, such as user preferences and behavioral performance, were collected on the chatbot platform to identify ways of providing personalized services.
The AI chatbots demonstrated potential for scalability by deployment through accessible devices and platforms (eg, smartphones and Facebook Messenger).

evidence.claim: Quality appraisal used CASP and CONSORT-AI
evidence.excerpt: AI techniques specific to AI chatbot interventions were also appraised using the CONSORT-AI (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials–Artificial Intelligence) extension guidance for AI studies

evidence.claim: Authors report validity and AI-description limitations
evidence.excerpt: the reported results need to be interpreted with caution because of the moderate to high risk of internal validity, insufficient description of AI techniques, and limitation for generalizability

evidence.claim: Primary outcomes are efficacy/feasibility, not governance
evidence.excerpt: Of the 15 included studies, several demonstrated the high efficacy of AI chatbots in promoting healthy lifestyles (n=6, 40%), smoking cessation (n=4, 27%)
